urgency.h: They're Betting You'll Just Go Away
urgency.sub: Employers fire people illegally every day for one reason: most people never call a lawyer. Don't be most people.

cards.p: Yes, California is an at-will state. No, that doesn't mean they can fire you for reporting harassment, taking medical leave, being pregnant, being over 40, or refusing to break the law. That's called wrongful termination — and it pays.

cards.t: The severance offer is a trap
cards.p: Two weeks' pay in exchange for signing away every claim you have? Employers don't offer severance out of kindness. They offer it because they know what a lawyer would find.
The glowing reviews before you complained. The schedule change after. The emails that prove the timing. Every week you wait, more of it disappears. A preservation letter from us stops the shredding.

results.label: Employment settlements by one partner since 2023

result_highlight: When an employer fires someone for an illegal reason, California law lets you recover back pay, front pay, emotional-distress damages, punitive damages, and your attorney's fees. The company that thought firing you was cheap is about to learn otherwise.

value.h: Wrongful Termination Isn't Just "Your Old Paycheck"
value.sub: People think a firing case is worth a few weeks of wages. Here's what the law actually puts on the table.

items.p: Every dollar you would have earned from the day they fired you until your case resolves — salary, overtime, commissions, bonuses, and the benefits that came with them.
The income you'll keep losing while you find comparable work. For senior roles or specialized careers, this is often the biggest number in the case.
Being fired illegally is humiliating and terrifying. Juries in California regularly award significant damages for what it did to your health, your family, and your peace of mind.
When a company fires you with malice — to punish you for speaking up, or to dodge a disability accommodation — the jury can award punitive damages meant to hurt.
Under the Fair Employment and Housing Act and other California laws, the employer pays your attorney's fees when you win. Which is exactly why we charge you nothing up front.

faq.q: What counts as wrongful termination in California?
faq.a: Being fired for an illegal reason — because of a protected characteristic (age 40+, race, gender, pregnancy, disability, religion, sexual orientation), in retaliation for complaining about harassment, discrimination, unpaid wages or safety violations, for taking protected medical or family leave, for refusing to do something illegal, or in breach of a contract. If the timing feels suspicious, it probably is.

faq.q: They gave me a reason. Doesn't that end it?
faq.a: No. Employers almost always give a reason — "performance," "restructuring," "budget." The question is whether it's the real reason. Years of good reviews followed by a sudden write-up after you complained is exactly what juries see through. We know how to prove pretext.

faq.q: Should I sign the severance agreement?
faq.a: Not before a free review. Severance agreements release every claim you have. Once we know what your case is worth, we can often negotiate a far larger severance — or turn a small offer into a real settlement.

faq.q: How long do I have to file?
How much is my wrongful termination case worth?
faq.a: It depends on your pay, how long you were there, how hard it is to replace your job, and how badly they behaved. Cases range from a few months' wages to seven figures. A free case review gives you a realistic range before you sign anything.

faq.q: Can I still file for unemployment?
faq.a: Yes — and you should. Filing for unemployment does not hurt your wrongful termination case, and if the employer contests it, what they say to the EDD often becomes evidence for us.
